question:
A rectangular grazing area is to be fenced off on three sides using part of a \(100\) meter rock wall as the fourth side. Fence posts are to be placed every \(12\) meters along the fence, including the two posts where the fence meets the rock wall. What is the fewest number of posts required to fence an area \(36\) m by \(60\) m?

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_8_Q18_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Equal spacing suggests counting the \(12\)-meter gaps first. The three fenced sides form one continuous path, with a post at each end where it meets the wall.

[Figure 1](figures/1986_AMC_8_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

A side against the wall can have length \(60\) meters or \(36\) meters. Both fit along the \(100\)-meter wall.

With a \(60\)-meter side against the wall, the fenced sides have total length
\[
36+60+36=132\text{ meters}.
\]
This gives \(132\div12=11\) gaps. Starting with the first post, each gap leads to one additional post, so there are \(11+1=12\) posts.

With a \(36\)-meter side against the wall, the fence length is
\[
60+36+60=156\text{ meters},
\]
requiring \(156\div12+1=14\) posts. In both arrangements, the side lengths are multiples of \(12\), so the spacing places posts at the corners, and each shared corner is counted just once along the continuous path.

These are the only two side lengths that can lie along the wall. Therefore the fewest posts required is \(\boxed{12}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

edges.reason: Describing rectangle and square properties presupposes recognizing which plane shapes those names designate.

Written columns support perimeter arithmetic with larger dimensions. Adding decomposed lengths mentally gives the same result even for two-digit sides, so Gemini's chosen calculation does not establish column-method necessity.
The perimeter formulas use rectangle opposite-side equality and square side equality to combine their boundary lengths.

The earlier one-digit long-division workflow is analogous but is not a mathematical suboperation needed to divide by a two-digit divisor. Division meaning, place value, trial products and subtraction suffice to learn the new workflow directly.
edges.scope: Familiarity with a similar long-division layout before learning two-digit divisors

edges.reason: Two-digit-divisor trial products multiply the divisor by one quotient digit, not two two-digit numbers. The two-by-two written product is broader useful practice rather than a prerequisite.
Line-segment and endpoint language supports the road-gap model. Placing counters along a concrete road picture also establishes the endpoint count without a prior line/ray taxonomy.
edges.scope: modeling the planting stretch with endpoints

edges.reason: Longer mixed calculations can help more elaborate planting counts. The stated endpoints-and-gaps relationships can be solved with a single small arithmetic step and do not mandate a three-step precedence workflow.
edges.scope: combining interval and count steps in one expression
